did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jeremiah uses the imagery of shepherds and sheep to criticize the leaders of the people: the shepherds are accused of scattering the flock and failing to care for it.

Did you know? Alongside his criticism of the leaders, the LORD promises to gather the remnant of his flock from all the countries and bring them back to pasture, where they will be fruitful and multiply.
Did you know? Jeremiah prophesies that a “righteous Branch” will be raised up for David—a king who will reign wisely and practice justice and righteousness in the land.
Did you know? The future redemption is described as such a great event that the exodus from Egypt will no longer be the primary way Israel remembers its deliverance.

Did you know? Jeremiah describes his reaction to the false prophets in powerful physical and emotional terms: his heart is broken, his bones tremble, and he feels like a drunken man because of the LORD and his holy words.
Did you know? The prophets of Samaria are accused of prophesying by Baal and leading Israel astray; thus, the chapter presents Baal worship and false prophecy as sources of the people’s downfall.

Did you know? Jeremiah establishes a standard for a true prophet by asking: Who has stood in the LORD’s council, listened to his word, and heard it? In this way, he distinguishes divine commission from personal claims.
Did you know? The chapter emphasizes the LORD’s all-encompassing presence: no one can hide from him, because he fills heaven and earth and sees what is done in secret.

Did you know? Jeremiah distinguishes between a dream reported by its owner and the true word of the LORD. He compares the word of the LORD to grain, in contrast to straw, to emphasize its value and truth.
Did you know? The word of the LORD is described through two powerful images: fire and a hammer that shatters a rock. These images express its power to penetrate, purify, and break through resistance.
